utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Please continue, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, General. This morning, we will try again the video-clip, 65 ter 45025. I hope that now we have a sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It functioned a few minutes ago. I don't know why it is not functioning. Yes, it doesn't work, so we have to give up on this one. Is there any explanation, why it is not working?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Court Deputy is inquiring. Shall we try again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's the second video, and obviously it is also not working again. If that cannot be fixed, it's a pity that we cannot hear what Dr. Karadzic is saying, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Audio/Video Unit is able to hear the sound at the booth, but we can't. They will find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Then let me move on, and we'll try at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The last topic, expulsion of population, I would like to address two documents. But before we do so: You mention in your statement that ethnic cleansing was a major topic at meetings with the Bosnian Serb leaders, and the term "ethnic cleansing," what did you understand it to entail?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, mike, microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you turn on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, is that clear? [Interpretation] I was referring to particular incidents. I did not use the term "ethnic cleansing." I was concerned with news and information we were receiving from the police and from the international Monitors of population -- of expulsion of Muslim populations, and I believe this was in the Gorazde region or something similar. And there is a report indicating that some 300 people were expelled from their homes. I wrote about this matter to the leadership. I explained that Muslim populations were being expelled from the Gorazde region. Some of them were resorting to one of the hotels in the region, and there were warnings that such matters were on the rise in other areas. I wanted the leadership to know that such incidents were happening so that they will put measures in place at higher levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you talked with the Bosnian Serb leadership about this practice, did they ever use the term "ethnic cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not use the term, as such, the term "ethnic cleansing," but I heard from them continuously or almost continuously in many of the meetings that there has been difficulty in living together with the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 01137 be brought up onto the screen, and the first page, please. And as it is coming up, it is a report of the special rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights, Tadeusz Mazowiecki, dated the 28th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, in your statement, in paragraph 52, you referred to this document as being one of those that you studied before you came to Sarajevo. And one more question to this. General, did you also review this document when you came here this weekend?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did so. Such documents and other documents were in the briefing that I received with General Nambiar at the beginning of my work with the United Nations in Sarajevo, and he said that, One of the problems you shall be facing is an increasing case of population expulsion from their homes, and these are one of the operations that should be stopped, because it prejudices our mandate in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 4 of the document, where we can see paragraph 7. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the header and in paragraph 7, it refers to the policy of ethnic cleansing pursued in the territories controlled by ethnic Serbs. While you were in Sarajevo, did you get information about such a policy and that it was occurring during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the problems that we were warning of continuously. I recall in one of the meetings, when we raised this issue with Madam Plavsic, she said, They Cannot live together and they have 500 families in Sarajevo that we would like to see outside Sarajevo because we are concerned for their lives and for their daily functions. And I said, This is totally contrary to our mission and the duties that we carry out, and such matters should be addressed at the political level and I am a military man.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we move on to page 6, where we can see paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Here in paragraph 17, it says, in relation to what was going on in Sarajevo: "The city is shelled on a regular basis, in what appears to be a deliberate attempt to spread terror among the population. Snipers shoot innocent civilians. The mission visited the hospital and was able to see many civilian victims. It was able to see damage done to the hospital itself, which has been deliberately shelled on several occasions, despite the proper display of the internationally-recognised Red Cross symbol." General, what the special rapporteur is writing here, did you see this reflected on the ground?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, the reports, whether those issued by the UNMOs or the UN police reports and the reports of the humanitarian organisations operating in the Sarajevo region, all reflected this painful situation; the sharp drop in the level and quality of daily life of the citizens and the injury to the necessary services, such as food and medication. There was terror on their faces, people were terrorised, and I felt people running in terror out of fear of snipers. And we, at the United Nations, we were also subject to sniping as we moved in the streets. Life was very bad and very desperate, especially for civilians in the Sarajevo region.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this regard, if you have a look at paragraph 18, it says here about the effect on the civilian population living in constant state of anxiety, leaving their homes and shelters only when necessary, and are seriously affected by the fighting and the siege. Were the inhabitants affected in that way, and did you make such observations?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and strongly so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we do that, I have some questions for the witness. General Abdel-Razek, the Prosecution referred to this document as the report of the special rapporteur, but on the first page it is written as "Letter from the Permanent Representative of the United States to the United Nations." Could you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are many documents that were distributed at various levels, starting from the field level in Sarajevo, in addition to copies of documents that were submitted to the UN. And copies of them were sent to the leadership in Zagreb, and I would receive copies of these reports as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So do you recognise this document as what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking of the situation. I have not gone into details as to this document, but I'm speaking of the case mentioned by the Prosecutor of the situation prevalent in Sarajevo. I am speaking specifically of the issues she raised as to Sarajevo, but I do not recall all the details. But what she mentioned, quoting this document about Sarajevo, is exactly similar to the situation that I lived through and other UN staff lived through in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'll hear from you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think this is a special situation because it's essentially a report of an investigation, and I would call the Trial Chamber's attention to the decision in the Milutinovic case, a decision on evidence tendered through Sandra Mitchell and Frederick Abrahams on the 1st of September, 2006, in which the Trial Chamber excluded evidence of Human Rights Watch investigators who had compiled a report concerning the atrocities in Kosovo. And I think that when we have evidence like this, which is essentially a report of someone else's investigation, that it's not proper for it to be admitted for its content without there being more showing of reliability and more adequate opportunity to confront this evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you do not challenge the authenticity of this document, which is a report of a special rapporteur on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, there's no question about its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Actually, this is a official UN document, despite the first few words here on this. It says it is a report of -- on the situation that the UN special rapporteur found on the ground. It was now confirmed in some parts by the witness. I can, of course, go through all paragraphs with this witness, and we will probably hear more about this, but I think that's sufficient, actually, to accept this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. And if I may, I believe that Mr. Robinson's citation is a bit misleading for a couple of reasons. First of all, the issue with respect to Mr. Abrahams was that he was introducing -- he was apparently seen as introducing individual statements of witnesses, as I recall, and eventually, further, Mr. Abrahams did testify about his report. So it did come in. The Mazowiecki report has come in repeatedly on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, really, isn't the evidence in this case -- and I'm sorry I'm addressing Mr. Tieger since he was the last to speak. The evidence in this case comes from the witness, the general. He is confirming factual situations which are reflected in the document, and to that extent the document is, in part, and if you like, an aide-memoire for the witness. It doesn't prove the document. It simply shows there is a consistency between what is in the document and that which the general recollects and can attest to. So if the document is admitted, it can only be admitted as part of it being consistent with this witness's testimony. It doesn't prove the document, as a whole, and it can't, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff pointed out, the document doesn't need to be proven through this witness. It's an official UN document, the authenticity of which is not contested. And I would urge that -- I appreciate the fact that if we -- focusing on the issues that Your Honour just mentioned, that logic is correct, but I'm confident that the Court wants the benefit of the best information it can get, the most comprehensive information it can get, in order to make the best decision possible. This report reflects the efforts of the international community, the special rapporteur. It's surely a document which the Court wishes to consider in its deliberations. It's been admitted in numerous cases. I urge the Court to admit it here for the reasons mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, that's -- I don't dispute that it's an official document, and there's no dispute that the document, I must speak now for myself, can be admitted for a limited purpose. The document may prove itself in the sense of its authenticity, but the mere fact of its admission doesn't prove each and every content of the document, and that needs to be attested to. And that's the issue which I was focusing upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understand that, and I fully appreciate the fact that the more information the Court has about the nature of any particular document, the way it was assembled, the particular details surrounding it, the greater weight the Court is going to be likely to give it. On the other hand, this is a case in which the Court will have the benefit of information from many sources, and, at the end of the case, will be assigning weight to any particular document on the basis of the totality of the evidence, which is why it's important to take those numerous strands, see where they intersect, and then determine at the conclusion of the case, on the basis of the totality of the evidence, what weight to give it. I'm confident that this Court, as other Courts, will be able to assess the appropriate weight to be given particular allegations in this document and particular information provided in this document when measured against the other evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, one more aspect. And we will actually show other UN reports of that kind and UN resolutions. Here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, let's move on. We've already spent too much time. This is an official UN document. The situation reflected in the document was confirmed by the witness. While it is a separate matter, what weight it is to be given pursuant to the late assessment, there's no problem in admitting this at this time. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a clarification. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, you referred to the witness's statement in which he allegedly said that ethnic cleansing was a major topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- tell me what paragraph it is?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. It is in paragraph 41 of that statement of 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we have the statement without para numbers. Page?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then I need to just -- it's on page 8, and it is the second-last paragraph, where the witness says this: "I recall --" it says here: "I recall that it was a major topic at almost every meeting I had with the Serb leadership." And he was referring to ethnic cleansing. It's the page R109 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I found it: "As to whether the term 'ethnic cleansing' had ever been used --"

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "-- during my meetings with the Bosnian Serb leaders, I recall it was a major topic at almost every meeting." Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 01629 be brought up on the screen. And as it is coming up: It is an occurrence report of UN Civilian Police Member Theriault of 30 September 1992, referring to the expulsion of 300 Muslim citizens from Grbavica Sector to the area of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: General, you mentioned a few minutes ago the 300 expelled Muslims, and is this report related to this event that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I believe this was -- this was one of the reports that I received from the police operating in the Sarajevo Sector. He came to my office in person, and he was disturbed by this incident. And I spoke about this incident in my meetings with the Serbian side, and especially in my meetings with Ms. Plavsic, and I said this sends very complex and disturbing messages, and instead of devoting our time to our duties, we will have to devote our attention to other duties, and such incidents are a shock to the international community. I mentioned this once and again in many of my meetings with her.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did she admit that this had happened and that she would do something about it, or what was her reaction?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, Ms. Plavsic often undertook to examine the matter. And I would hold a second meeting with her to hear from her, but then she would raise other issues and would not give definitive answers to all the questions that are raised in former meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I intervene once again. General, this is just a clarification. In transcript page 3, line 4, General, you said that -- it's about the ethnic cleansing, I quote: "No, they did not use the term, as such, the term 'ethnic cleansing,' but I heard from them continuously, or almost continuously, in many of the meetings that there had been difficulty in living together with the population." But Judge Lattanzi is saying that what she heard in French translation was a bit different, so could you clarify? Who had difficulty with whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The term of -- hardship of living together I would hear from my meetings with the Serb leadership. They often repeated the term or the expression that they were finding difficulty now in living together and there should be different arrangements put in place. And they had a map in colours which gave these parts to the Muslims and this part to the Croats and that part to the Serbs, and in one of them -- they don't deny this. In one of the meetings, they gave me this map, they handed me a copy. And they would consider this to be the ideal way to address the problem after the situation flared up and reached the point of blood-drenched conflict. But I did not use the term "ethnic cleansing" as an expression in English. I was speaking of the expulsion of the population, the population of a certain ethnic origin, as an event that I saw before my eyes, with very clear features. But as a general policy practiced all over Yugoslavia, this I cannot address. I speak of what I heard in my headquarters, incidents that disturbed those working with me, and they described these incidents in detail; expulsion of population in a certain area, in the Gorazde region. This is the area we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Back to you, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We give it one more try to have the video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that they will try during the break. So if you don't mind, we can revisit, during the course of cross-examination, with the indulgence of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, then, that concludes my examination-in-chief. I would now request that the associated exhibits referred in the statement of 16 July be admitted into evidence. They form an indispensable and inseparable part of the general's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence? Just one minor observation. It relates to the 65 ter number 40003, which is a video-clip of meeting, General Abdel-Razek with General Galic, but I don't -- I can't find the reference to the document in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is a reference, but I would not insist on this particular exhibit because it basically shows -- it confirms simply that the witness met General Galic, yes. That's not -- I would not insist on this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But the other ones are all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- 65 ter 08656, and I couldn't find the reference to this in the statement. I was advised that this is a duplicate of 65 ter number 11352. In any event, where is this referred to in his statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: 656 is referred in -- on page R109-1986, at paragraph 5. And I have actually checked them all, and it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the page number?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me see. It's page number 11. And when you look at the second-last paragraph, there is a reference to a document of 10 October. It's the document that we are talking about, UNPROFOR report sent to Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it says: "I made a report to Professor Koljevic." It's a report to Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me just see. It's about -- oh, oh, sir, it's about a conversation with Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in his conversation with Professor Koljevic, he referred to this UN document?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's -- let me just see where I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam, but that's not clear from the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just can't find the document right now in my binder, but I would double-check. But I checked it all, and it was, indeed, correct. But I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So subject to further clarification in relation to 8656, and you withdraw 40003, on that basis we'll admit them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the proper exhibit number will be circulated in due course by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Morrison has one further question for the witness before the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: General, sir, "salam alaikum." I was wondering if you could clarify. What was the composition of your staff that you were commanding, in terms of numbers and relative ranks, and what was your ability to move around the city of Sarajevo? How easy or how difficult was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as a matter of fact, the structure of the UN force in Sarajevo was as follows: The command of the force, which was located at what was called the PTT building; there, the commander, the deputy commander, the chief of staff of the sector, the Operations Centre and the Liaison Office, and the Administrative and Financial Office, the Office of the Political Adviser, as well as an administrative support company, communication company. The Administrative Company was French. The Communication Company was Dutch. And there was also a medical company, which was French. They were all deployed there, and that was the main structure of the sector command. All of the officers were professional. Some of them were staff officers and they had deep-seated experience in running such kind of operations. They also had a deep experience in working for the United Nations. The main force was the French Battalion, which was deployed in the Sarajevo Airport. There was also the Ukrainian Battalion, which was deployed in the Barracks of Tito. There was also the Egyptian Battalion, which was deployed in a B District area. The operations were all organised inside the city of Sarajevo. My movement was totally limited and confined to such areas, from the headquarters to the airport, to check on the French Battalion, and from there we were able to have access to other areas, such as Pale, Jurina [as interpreted], and other areas. We extended our operations to the Kiseljak area, where we set up -- where the Bosnian forces were set up under the leadership of Mr. Morillon, and I could get there through Validja [as interpreted] to the area of Kiseljak. As far as my communications were concerned and my movements were concerned, I think my movements were limited from the centre of command, to the Presidency, to the areas where the battalions were deployed, and to the hospital. My movements were limited. I was not in a situation that permitted me to move around Sarajevo beyond the areas that were of our own interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. That gives us a much better idea. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I double-checked with the document that we just spoke about. In this 10 October 1992 report, when you look at the second page, there is, indeed, a discussion described with Professor Koljevic and how he and Ms. Plavsic dealt with matters, and that's what the witness was actually speaking about. And so the first line of the statement is a bit misleading, but that's the report that deals with Koljevic and Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We didn't read that with that care. With that understanding, that will be admitted as well. Mr. Karadzic, now it's your turn to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I'm sorry that that video footage could not be played, but at least we did get to see how much younger we were 18 years ago. Thank you, General, for having met up with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll see the video after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for having met up with the Defence, and thank you for having given us the opportunity of clarifying certain matters that had been unclear. I already see how your very specific testimony is of assistance to the Trial Chamber. They can see the very essence of what was going on. However, multiple interpretation leads to a certain lack of precision. Also, I'd like to thank you for having agreed on various matters during that interview, and that will make it possible to make this cross-examination shorter. Do you agree that at that time, you and I had a very good co-operation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. [Interpretation] No, I did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we try again. Could you read -- shall I read it or could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can actually repeat it. However, let us establish whether the general is receiving interpretation in the first place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear the Arabic translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I shall repeat what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I expressed my gratitude to you for having accepted to meet with the Defence and help the Defence clarify certain matters. I said that multiple interpretation into several different languages leads to certain ambiguities. We saw yesterday how there was that mistake in respect of "call" and "appeal," and that considerably changes the meaning of the text involved. I believe that we agreed on certain matters during the interview, so I would like to refer to them now. We did agree, didn't we, that at the time while you were there for six months, you and I had a very good co-operation; right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer this? Well, if I can make a comment. I repeatedly said that my meetings with the leadership were generally good and there was good atmosphere that prevailed on the meetings. We talked about things that were of interest to everyone, and I deemed that the atmosphere that prevailed on the meeting was very good. And I would like to leave aside some very important topics, and in order to -- I say that in general. I said precisely that my meetings with the leadership were met with great respect. They showed respect to me and to the United Nations, in general. And I say that we were in a good situation among ourselves, but the problem was in the field. Whenever we went to the field to see whether the points of agreement that we reached with the leadership were implemented on the ground, well, sometimes we were faced with hardships on the ground, so the problem is that in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo, in general, the problem was in the practices on the ground. The problem was not in our meetings with the leadership, the problem was not in our talks with the leadership. Those talks took place in a positive atmosphere. However, what was on the ground was not at all acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The translation we received -- part of the translation is like this: It's line 19: "And I would like to leave aside some very important topics and in order to ... I say that in general." Is something missing from that translation, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I am following the interpretation, and the interpretation is precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. However, one can say that in spite of the difficult topics we had to deal with, can you say that you did reach agreement with us and that you never really left our meetings empty-handed, as it were?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I said that repeatedly, that all my meetings with you were positive, we all came out from those meetings happy, we all agreed on opening the roads, removing the roadblocks, and stopping the shelling of Sarajevo and stopping any hindrance to the movements of the United Nations. The meetings looked happy, looked good, and I came out of the meetings happy, hopeful that we -- that the results would be positive. However, the problems continued. The shelling intensified. Roadblocks were increased. And I complained about that situation many times to you or to General Mladic in the course of our meetings, and I reported those complaints to General Galic, who was the operational commander of the sector. But I heard so many positive words from you and from Mr. Galic; however, that was contrary to what happened on the ground. And I would like to say the same thing in answering all the questions that are asked on this matter. I would like to say that our meetings with the leadership were all positive, a positive atmosphere prevailed at all the meetings, and we were all hopeful at the end of those meetings that something positive would be implemented on the ground. However, the facts on the ground were contrary to what we had agreed upon. So while that perhaps could be a result of the lack of any pressure on the soldiers on the ground, or there was probably a failure in the control/command system, so I didn't really know why the agreements were not implemented. So I say again that the meetings were positive. However, the practices on the ground were something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that most of our agreements were actually implemented? At the meeting we had, you expressed exceptional understanding for the nature of our civil war. You said that it was a war where everybody fought everybody, where neighbours fought neighbours, and so on. I believe it would be a good thing if you would tell the Trial Chamber what this kind of a civil war is like, where there are different components involved, where everybody has weapons, where everybody could buy weapons, and when there was mutual fear on the ground. We discussed that during the interview, and I believe that you understood that very well.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I received a brief -- well, it wasn't a brief, actually. It was a detailed report on the situation in Sarajevo from General Nambiar, and they told me about the situation -- the nature of the situation in Sarajevo. I did know that, and as I said, that I received reports from the United Nations, I had a meeting with the Yugoslav ambassador to Angola, and I received a number of documents from Mr. Goulding. I also received information from the media. So I was privy to the nature of the conflict there. As General Nambiar put it, it was a civil war. The neighbours fought about the neighbours, the civilians fought against the military. We cannot really pin-point any particular party. I know that everybody had strong feelings about that, and that was the nature of war. But we were -- I said that we had a humanitarian mission in Sarajevo aimed at keeping the airport open for humanitarian aid and to protect and guard humanitarian convoys, and extend help and assistance to the civilians in the conflict area. As for the conflict, itself, I think it's something political, and our -- and it is the interest of the politicians. Our role was a field role to provide what I said we were there for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While discussing the difference between what had been agreed upon and what actually happened on the ground, during our interview you expressed a certain degree of understanding. You actually said that you did not blame the leaders for that, because you said that that was the nature of war. Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a military, and I took part in four Middle Eastern wars, I know that the situation was not peaceful. I was not monitoring a cease-fire or a peace agreement among the parties to the conflict. Our assignment was limited. We were in a time of war. Weapons were used against civilians, but what interested me most was the use of heavy weapons against civilians. I wanted to make sure that the United Nations forces had access to all areas and that they were able to carry out their mission of protecting the civilians. So anything contrary to that or anything that hindered that mission was of my interest, and that was raised by me in the meetings. So I said there was understanding by the leadership of our mission, but, however, the command and control on their part was not enough in the field, and I think there was a failure of communication to the -- between the higher leadership and the leadership on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. It seems to me that we agreed that during the implementation of our agreements with the other side, especially with regard to supplies and infrastructure, that one of the main problems was the danger or the attempt to have one side secure military or strategic supremacy while the agreement was being implemented, and that that was a considerable hindrance in the process. Right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not really understand the question. Could you clarify the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm now going through what we agreed upon during the interview. Did we agree that in the implementation of our agreements with you and with the other side, especially with regard to humanitarian affairs and infrastructure repairs, a particular hindrance was the possibility that one side would try to gain a strategic or tactical advantage and that that hindered the implementation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was interested in, and I say that I'm not -- I wasn't really concerned with who was trying to impose their supremacy in there - there was a war - what I was interested in is that the area was important, and we wanted to repair the infrastructure so that the basic necessities were provided; electricity, gas, and water, et cetera. I said that those basic necessities were not available in the area, and that was a hindrance to and exacerbated the situation. We were directly affected. There was a time when, for 15 days, I wasn't able to take a shower. The situation was extremely difficult. We used electric generators to get electricity. So you have to imagine the situation in the hospitals and the other parts of the city. I was mostly interested in the results. I wanted to make sure that the agreements entered into were fully implemented. However, the agreements were reached in a very positive atmosphere. We all agreed to find -- to find a solution to the situation. However, that was contrary to the practices on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now briefly like to emphasise what we had agreed on in the interview. I hope you can answer this question by saying yes or no, and then we can move on to more essential things. You confirmed that when a high-level foreign official would arrive, there were so-called welcomes, a sort of shelling, in fact, and that was the case when you arrived there, too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak for what happened with every other senior official that arrived. I can speak for myself, what happened with me. When Mr. Owen or Mr. Vance or the Secretary-General arrived on a visit, the situation seemed to be calm, but I remember, when I first arrived, there were fireworks and I had spent the whole evening in the bunker. I remember the shelling then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that when going to Sarajevo -- well, in a certain statement, it seems that you said that Sarajevo was destroyed. But in the interview, we clarified this matter, and, in fact, it was said that most of the suburbs of Sarajevo were destroyed, whereas the center -- in the center, some big buildings had been destroyed or damaged; the "Oslobodjenje" building, for example, and so on and so forth; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said when I moved from the airport to HQ, I was surprised at the level of destruction that I saw, and I noticed that several civilian areas were hard hit by the shelling. And the following day after my arrival, I was on a quick tour with Mr. Izetbegovic, and I could see the extent of damage caused by the shelling; glass shards, marks of shrapnel on the buildings. I did not say that the city was completely destroyed, but I noticed that there was an extensive level of damage, and especially in the move from the airport to my headquarters. We have to also say that when there is no aerial bombardment, the level of destruction cannot be as extensive as people try to portray it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do we agree that you confirmed that the extensive damage mainly concerned the suburbs of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I have to re-state what I said. During my movement from the airport to the city, I noticed that some villages or townships on the outskirts had sustained extensive damage and there are clear signs of heavy shelling in the direction of these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of the interview, you said that foreign governments or, rather, Presidencies were angry with you, there was a campaign in the media against you, because they expected you to do something that wasn't part of your mandate; is that correct? You can answer this question by simply say yes or no, General.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said this. What I said clearly at the time, that in the final days of my mission and as a result of the operations in the Otes area, I arrived at the conclusion that we have not been able to achieve much. We found ourselves in the same situation as the civilians, who were caught in the city, and I said that clearly in a press conference. This is well documented. And certain circles felt the frustration in my statement, and I did not have to hide that frustration. And after six months in the city, in charge of the mission, I was sleeping no more than four or five hours, and that press conference, in specific, contained a tone of anger. I have to admit that, because I felt that we found ourselves in a situation where we were not delivering, and a military man, I felt that I should not be there and that it was a waste of time and that I could not continue in this role with the UN. The Secretary-General of the UN felt that tone of anger and raised the issue with General Nambiar. General Nambiar explained to the Secretary-General that I was feeling frustrated, that I was coming under a lot of pressure. And I -- at that time, I made it clear that the UN needs to find a replacement for me because I have decided to call it a day. I was not reacting in anger towards anybody, any party, any state. My reaction was to the ability to deliver or not. And there were situations where I tried to do my best to relieve the pressure on certain circles, and people were evacuated to Split, and I believe that operation went smoothly. The only failure that I still feel sour about is not being able to retrieve the three UN drivers that were -- who were abducted. Apart from that, I don't have any qualms about anything I did during my mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't have you in mind, but you also were under pressure that was exerted on you by other sides. Did you confirm that it was in the interests of the SDS [as interpreted] leadership to provoke a foreign intervention? SDA, not the SDS. The SDA leadership. The transcript says "the SDS."

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that was my personal feeling. Nobody prompted me or nobody alluded to me about that. So what with all the shelling and the deprivation the civilians were facing, and not seeing any glimmer of hope after the presence of the United Nations forces, that led me to the conviction or to the belief that the civilians wanted international intervention, wanted the international community to step in. Nobody told me this, but that's how I felt. And that brings me again to the reference to ethnic cleansing, how that was perceived, and words were trying -- somebody was trying to put words into my mouth. That's not what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You agreed, did you not, that the fire opened on two UNPROFOR soldiers came from Butmir, under the control of the ABiH, and you protested about this to Ganic and Izetbegovic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is clearly stated in my report. Any side to the conflict, any party that tried to inflict damage or hamper the work of UN, I took the case to that party. There was this convoy moving from Lukavica towards the airport. Fire was opened on the convoy, and as a result of opening fire, two drivers died. I reacted quickly, an inquiry commission was set up. And we were trying to establish the direction of fire, and we arrived at the conclusion that the source of the fire came from the direction where the Bosnian troops were positioned. I was not able to meet Mr. Izetbegovic at the time, so I met with Mr. -- with Mr. Ganic, and I made it clear that we have reason to believe that the fire opened came from directions where their troops were positioned. I made that abundantly clear to him, and all the witnesses present, like other drivers on the convoy and their assistants, agreed on the fact that Butmir was the source of fire. And I made it clear, then, that there is no point in trying to deny this, and I made it clear to them that this is a clear violation of the agreement which is intended to provide protection for UN convoys from all the parties to the conflict. And I think everybody knows how strict and firm I was when it came to that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise, I'm waiting for the interpretation to end. You agreed with us that as opposed to foreign embassies [as interpreted], governments, and their sides, the Serbian sides never positioned their mortars or artillery near UN positions in order to provoke retaliation against the UN; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one thing I'm certain about with my subordinates. We did not have any shelling of the UN headquarters, but I could hear also shelling coming out from the premises of the UN HQ, which was supposed to be a 500-metre radius. I went to see the other side, and I explained to them, I heard the rounds being fired from the proximity of the UN building. And I made clear that as a result of these rounds fired from the proximity of the UN, there was a response to that fire, and we, as UN people, we were getting the return fire. But at some stage or after a while, this came to an end, because these mortars were mounted on flatbed trucks and they were positioned in the vicinity of our location, and they used to fire and run away. And, as a result, the PTT building got hit by the return fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, since you can understand English, is your question translated correctly? Did you say "as opposed to foreign embassies"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Excellency. "As opposed to Bosnian forces," the forces of the Bosnian government. You noticed that correctly, and I believe that the general also understood what was at stake. Could we have the following document, 1D02175, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is one of a series of documents. There are a number of documents that relate to what you have just said and also that relate to the shelling of those settlements through which you passed. Do you remember the Nedzarici settlement?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that we have certain problems with the e-court system as well, so we will show this document after the break. It seems that I didn't read this out correctly. 1D01275 is the number of the document which should be up on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Nedzarici settlement was an exclusively Serbian settlement?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it's difficult for me to determine, after all this time, whether this area was exclusively Serb or Bosniak. I cannot say that with certitude. But I don't know where you're getting -- what you're getting at from that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Please have a look at the translation of this document. This is a document from the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ABiH. It's a conversation between an UNPROFOR representative and a representative of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you know General Hosen? I'm not quite sure how you pronounce that name.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I deal with a number of the leadership on the other side, and there are other people with them, their deputies, their assistants, and I cannot remember all the names. When I met with General Galic, and he was accompanied by other officers whose names I cannot recall, I cannot remember. But when I entered a conversation, I entered a conversation with the -- with my interlocutor, with the commander that is on the same level with me, but I do not know the names of other people accompanying that person. [In English] Sorry, sorry, sorry. [Interpretation] Excuse me. This is the first time I see this document. The document seems to be the minutes of a meeting. I have reason to believe that the reference to Hussein here is myself. This is a reference to me. I believe I met with Mr. Cibo. If we go back to the document, I remember we were late for that meeting because we lost our way. We end up going to the command centre of a different unit, and there we were told that this is not the place where the meeting was supposed to take place. And when we arrived late, he was not happy at all, and I tried to explain the unfortunate incident. And I have reason to believe that the reference to Hussein in that document is a specific reference to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, excellent. So please have a look at the enlarged part. It's in the middle of the text. You say that the UN wants to establish peace, they want the guns to remain silent, they want the song of peace to be heard, and so on and so forth. And you say: "Today at 3.00, French soldiers in Nedzarici were wounded." And then you say: "With regard to position, 500 metres from our positions, there were mortars that were firing from the vicinity of the PTT building. The Serbs responded and hit a position near our building. There were no victims." And you say: "A distance of 500 metres should be respected." He says that: "We've already ordered this." And then you say: "We received from London, from the Serbs, confirmation that in a certain number of hours, UNPROFOR will be provided with access." So we have to see how this is translated: "They will be provided with the possibility of examining all the positions where there's heavy artillery around Sarajevo," and so on and so forth. And then you say this is from major -- prime minister, major, and so on. Do you remember this part of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, when I go to a meeting of this type, there is an agreed agenda, the points to be discussed, and this agenda is given to the liaison officers from both sides. The agenda is sent out prior to the meeting for the collection of information and preparation. These are the issues that were raised in all meetings with all the -- when I met with Commander Siber, or Siber, that was one of the issues that were on the agenda, and I can say, yes, these are -- these are issues that could have been the topics that were raised during that meeting. And I have reason to believe that these -- this information is accurate because the Bosnian side had a note-taker, and the same thing applies to the UN side. We took notes of the proceedings of the meeting so that we can base our decisions on the issues raised before we report back to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So here you say: "This is according to the orders issued by major from London. We can't force any of the sides to do anything. You need goodwill here." Then General Siber says that the Serbs are losing in certain places, and then there is retaliation against the civilians. And you remain silent about that for a long time, and then you say: "This agreement is from the London Conference, and it's the other side's obligation, too. I'll discuss the matter with them, and I will draw up a plan on this agreement. If we reach an agreement, I will inform you of the fact, and if not, I'll inform you of that fact too." And so on and so forth. And then Mr. Siber says that they need occasional cease-fires in shifts, he says - I'm not quite sure how that was translated - so that the engineers could repair electricity supplies, water supplies, and the heating system and so on. Or, in fact, that's what you say. And then he says: "I'm sorry that your men have been wounded, but what were they doing in Nedzarici, where the fighting was intense?" And you say: "They were escorting a convoy," and so on. So if I remind you of the fact that Nedzarici is the exit from the airport, from Kasindolska Street, do you remember that the houses there are low houses, private houses, and there are no military installations there, and shelling at Nedzarici amounted to terrorising the civilian population there?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to be more precise? You are making references to certain statements, but I don't know exactly who are you referring to, having said that. I would -- there were points that were raised by both sides in a meeting. For example, if you were to say to me there were soldiers who were injured in the process, yes, I can understand that, because fighting was going on and you expect people to get injured. But I am not clear exactly on who said what from that statement. During these meetings, meetings of this type, I entered into the same conversation not only with one side, whether with General Siber or even with General Galic, and here I'm talking about the commands -- the military commands of both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, could I ask you to have a look at the following sentence: "We will report anything to the Supreme Command ..." And so on and so on. [In English] And he said: "I am sorry that your people were wounded, but what they doing in Nedzarici, where fierce battles are underway?" [Interpretation] So your soldiers were in Nedzarici. They were escorting a humanitarian convoy. At the time, they attacked Nedzarici, and that was pointless. All they could do was kill them and destroy that settlement. There was no other reason. So he says, What were your soldiers doing there? So this is proof that they attacked Nedzarici and accidentally killed and wounded French soldiers. And you say they were escorting a humanitarian convoy, and he says, No one said that there should be a cease-fire. So they are shelling a Serbian settlement in Sarajevo, and your soldiers happened to be there. Can you see that paragraph now?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is how matters were. An indication of French soldiers getting hit, they were not protecting a convoy. This is was the UN convoy that was coming from Bacevo, and this convoy came over regular periods periodically to extend to our sector or our needs. And the shooting against this convoy is what was being referred to in this meeting, I believe. Therefore, they were not protecting the convoy. They were French drivers within the convoy of munitions, of administrative munitions. Many things were said, and I replied accordingly. This was a dialogue, a dialogue between me and the commander. I don't recall the details, but such matters happened all the time, continuously, in my meetings with the different commanders in the Sarajevo region.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D501, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm noting the time. We'll have a break. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we begin with watching that video you wanted to show us?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It seems to be working now, and that's the video-clip 65 ter 45025.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "I went 'round the hospital in Sarajevo today, and I -- which is very, very, very depressing. I don't expect these days to have to go into the recovery room and find a shell that's gone through it, of the recovery ward. I went completely unannounced. I didn't tell anybody. I didn't take any press, I didn't make anything of it. I just went as a doctor." "Mistake, because on the agreement, it was you. It was a case of cessation of hostilities."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we spoke about it already yesterday, so we don't need to go into details anymore, except for one question, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did this meeting take place, and do you recall when, approximately, that was?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall exactly, but it was during the crisis, during the shelling. We always received visits from the representative of the European Community, Mr. Owen, and the representative of the Secretary-General, Mr. Vance, and the Secretary-General personally as well. I believe during this meeting that followed the intensive shelling of the city, including the vicinity of the hospital, in fact, he did go there, himself. It was not a scheduled visit. I recall this. But before we moved from Sarajevo to attend this meeting, he informed us that he had gone by the vicinity of the hospital and had met with the physicians and listened to them. This matter left an unfavorable impression on him, and I believe he raised this issue at the beginning of the talks in the meeting hall. And I can see, in this meeting, the staff of the Serbian leadership, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic and General Mladic, and I also see, on the UN side, Mr. Morillon and myself, sitting to the left of Mr. Owen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to request admittance of this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Only this part?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, only this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I forgot to note the time-frame when you started, but we can note the end of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We started at 1:34:33, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To 01:35:30. Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P1273, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And then the next video-clip, it is 65 ter 45015, and it should now be working.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "On the other hand, Muslims, we know that, and we have to say to the Muslim people, finally, when everything will be settled, we will sue some men who had done this, who were bombarding Sarajevo, the Muslims, with the Muslim Army, who are placing the explosions on the streets of Sarajevo to kill their own people to accuse Serbs. These things are already detected. Everybody in the world is laughing. When somebody, for example, some dignitary is coming, and then the bombs fall, vehicle and some -- and some mine -- well, mortar hits the Presidency, everybody is laughing, everybody knows it's show time. "So if Mr. Greg comes -- Greg from the United Nations - I don't know if you saw this statement - said that Serbs have enough artillery in reserve around the city that they could demolish Sarajevo 10 times, to level Sarajevo with the ground, but they do not use it. They do not want to. That is what Colonel Greg said. But we do not want to conquer Sarajevo. We do not want to tear down Sarajevo. Sarajevo is our city, too. But, please, when somebody puts a mortar artillery weapon on some skyscraper and it is hitting us, hitting us, and kills 25 of our men in one day, so to say we must hit this to neutralise it. "People from Sarajevo who got out have told me they knew exactly what would happen to their building. When they hear shooting from their building, they know that within half an hour to 45 minutes, Serbs will have to neutralise that, and then they're going to the basement. So housing objects, religious objects in Sarajevo are turned into military objects, and forces us when we become threatened, our lives, we have to answer to neutralise that. We are hitting their recoilless guns. Their mortars are neutralised, and they are showing it to the world and trying to cause sympathy and compassion."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I don't know where it started, but it's 00:01:37.8. And where did it start?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, Colonel, to your knowledge -- sorry. General, to your knowledge, did the Bosnian government forces have artillery weapons on skyscrapers?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not believe that artillery can be used in such a way, for it has a strong reaction once it is fired, and this means that artillery is usually accompanied by hydraulic means to absorb the shock of firing. So it is not rationale to have such artillery on the top of high buildings. This is something no professional person would believe. You could have light mortar-launchers, perhaps, but not more. I haven't seen this or heard this. All that I recall is that small mortars or light mortars are sometimes used on semi vehicles, mobile-launcher that would fire and then move, and this is in guerrilla warfare. All this is possible. But heavy artillery on top of high buildings, that I cannot imagine.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And my last question: Did you ever get information or find evidence that the Muslims placed explosives in the streets to kill their own people, to accuse later on the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, so many claims were made by so many of the parties. What bothered us most was these claims and counter-claims. I cannot imagine that you could have explosives planted on roadsides, because these have to be timed, they should have a timer, or they would have a detonator and the person hiding somewhere, and when the convoy passes -- so it's a complex operation. We did not come across this all throughout the period of my stay in Sarajevo, but I did hear many claims from one side against the other side to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, can this video be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this clip immediately followed the previous part --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- so it should have started from 01:37: --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- no, 01:35:30, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, 0:09:52, that's where it started, and it ended at 00:11.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What we are seeing now is at 00 --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's from the original video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't know why these here are differently. Oh, this is a clip from the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit this clip?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be Exhibit P1274, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Back to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I would agree with you regarding heavy artillery. However, I don't know whether the interpretation was right. I'm talking about mortars and recoilless guns. Are you familiar with the weapon we had, recoilless gun? There is no shock involved, as the name, itself, says, "recoilless."

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, these recoilless guns is an anti-tank weapon, and it is fired horizontally and you cannot fire it from high locations, for usually it is used against tanks and against personnel carriers. These are recoilless guns, but I do not think it is practical to place them over high buildings. They would be of no use. But I could imagine having certain mortar-launchers on some of the roofs, particularly the low-calibre ones, not the high-calibre ones.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since we were dealing with Lord Owen, anyway, now we're going to see what Lord Owen says about these topics. 1D144, we are going to play that, and I would like to ask the Registrar to have this video handed over to the OTP. Although we played this during our opening statement, however, I'd like to have it played now as well. We burned that particular section that's going to be played so that the OTP can have their own copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "There's no use anybody pretending that they are innocents in this business and that there is one side that's pure white, the victims, and the other side --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This time, we have sound, but ... Can we move on to another topic while we can check the status of the video? While we are waiting, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, the exhibit tendered as 65 ter number 8656, I forgot that it was -- to note that it was noted in your filing that it should be tendered under seal. Could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the documents that we had from the UN were not actually to be under seal. I think there was a particular reason, perhaps, in that previous case, why this was done; (redacted) So to my knowledge, it's not a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will delete that part referring to the witness, but we'll just -- we'll admit it publicly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting, can we have D13 -- rather, 351 in e-court. D351. I believe that that's the document. Can we please have page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember the time concerned and this document? General Morillon is writing to Mr. Izetbegovic about breaking of Geneva Convention. Do you remember this letter? We showed this to you during the interview, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I could almost say with certitude that there was correspondence written by me or by General Morillon to inform of any breaches by any party. We did not focus on one party. We worked in total neutrality. Whatever we witnessed, we wrote about to the relevant parties in Sarajevo, and we informed the leadership in Zagreb as well. This is not the only document of this kind. There are numerous other documents related to violations, whether minor or major violations here or there. This is a very normal part of our work in the United Nations system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We here have a document included that shows that in the yard of the Kosevo Hospital, there was -- there was a mortar battery that was permanently positioned there. And here, Morillon, General Morillon, protested. The second paragraph says that a shell had been launched from the hospital, itself. Nine shells had been launched from that position, and afterwards there was retaliation, and this was a cowardly act, firing from the hospital was a cowardly act, provoking such retaliation. It was a cowardly act, and it served to accuse the other side, obviously. So this is a matter that Lord Owen addressed; isn't that correct? He said that fire was opened on the hospital, and General Morillon established that, first of all, fire was opened from the position of the hospital, and then the Serbs were accused of having targeted the hospital; isn't that correct? General, you can answer this very briefly. With regard to what Lord Owen said at the time, does this concern the incident that we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall from Lord Owen and what he said, I said yesterday that he was a diplomat and he presented his positions in a very diplomatic manner, without provoking the other side. This was his nature in all his dealings. Even when he was addressing the Presidency, he used such language. This was his language in all his consultations. I, as a military man, I can say that such matters are claims. We heard these claims from the party of General Galic and as well as from the Bosnian side. Each party tried to justify why they committed this error. And I would focus in my talks with General Galic and say, Okay, I will accept that there are forces that are positioned in certain places, but you should be wise. You should not retaliate against areas where there are many civilians. You can retaliate somewhere else along the front, but to attack areas where there are civilians, and this is a mistake and it brings major injuries, and it hurts us and hurts public opinion, because, in brief, there are civilians getting killed and there are humanitarian facilities and hospitals that are getting destroyed and unable to function, so they should move away from shelling any civilian population centres. If they want to carry out military activities, they can do this in a professional manner in other areas. And I do not want to prolong now on this, but there are so many claims and counter-claims on so many different activities. Each party tries to clean its hands of the claims directed against them from the other party, and that this was only in retaliation against what hit us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm concerned about the way you conduct your cross-examination. This is the document we admitted when a protected witness came, and you put this document to the witness. It's okay for you to put this document in a brief manner. General Abdel-Razek confirmed this document, and then you proceeded to read out all the contents of this document, and then which triggered another lengthy answer from the witness, which I find unnecessary. So bear that in mind in the future. And, General, if you could answer the question with "yes" or "no," please do so. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In relation to this document, General, your services or General Morillon established that there was a mortar in Kosevo Hospital and there were at least nine shells that were fired at Serb positions; isn't that right? Just "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, personally, did not say so. I did not say that there was a mortar-launcher in the vicinity of the hospital. We went often to this hospital, and I personally did not see this. And I do receive information from monitors in the sector, and we did not receive information as to having such mortar-launchers in the vicinity of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. The document is self-explanatory, but let me ask you something else, General. You're a soldier, and if your unit is suffering losses from one particular firing position, are you going to retaliate somewhere else or will you try to silence the weapon that has inflicted all these losses -- heavy losses on you?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a military leader, I would retaliate. But where, that's my choice, and my choice has to be wise. I do not want to retaliate just out of vengeance, but I want to retaliate in a professional manner and to direct my weapon or my military activity not necessarily at the same position. We, as military men, we know that if this engagement is leading to losses, I can incur losses -- I can bring about losses in other areas. And I can avoid the shelling of sensitive civilian positions, and everybody knows what I mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, General Morillon is objecting to Izetbegovic about breaches of the Geneva Conventions, so they're the ones who violated the Geneva Convention. Theirs is the responsibility for placing mortars in a civilian zone. So the party that did that is to be blamed; right? Just yes or no. Is he responsible for placing that in the civilian zone, and is he not using the civilians as a human shield in order to inflict pain on the other side? Is that legitimate or not?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is not at normal front-line. This was a front-line in a large city. What does it mean, to use civilians? They are part of the game of war. And I, personally -- and as for the UN agreement with the different parties, the UN wanted to avoid fighting among civilians, and to open the roads, and not to have UN convoys subject to fire, and not to have its facilities attacked. If anything came counter to this aim, we would address all the relevant parties. And this document speaks in the same spirit. This is the same issue that I would present to General Galic and to Colonel Siber. So it comes in the context of the document that was submitted earlier for the objection to Colonel Siber on some of the operations that affected the United Nations forces and some of the civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D01157, please. Could we have that in e-court, 1D01157.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 23rd of September, 1992. You had been in Sarajevo for a month already; right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the date, yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to draw to your attention and to the attention of all participants this paragraph that is marked here: "During General Morillon's stay at the barracks in Lukavica ..." And you see how many provocations there were. We responded. That is what you called those games of war; right? Allow me to read this through: "At the time of General Morillon's stay at the Slobodan Princip Seljo Barracks in Lukavica, the enemy attacked Vojkovici and Dobrinja with mortar fire. Our units were ordered not to return fire. A combined infantry and artillery attack, started yesterday by the enemy from the Ilijas Misaca [phoen] Sector, continued today." And then it says General Morillon -- "From 9.30 to 1100 hours this morning, General Morillon visited the Ilidza sector where he talked with the commander of the Ilidza Brigade and with the president of the municipality," and so on and so forth. "Losses: four soldiers were lightly wounded. "We didn't respond." Does this tally with what you can remember and with the knowledge you have of the way in which people acted in that area?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall we went to Ilidza when General Morillon came to open a command post for the UN forces in Bosnia. And we went to Ilidza. And my advice to him was not to be inside Sarajevo so that he will have freedom of mobility. I told him, Either you go to Ilidza or you go to any other area. So we went to Ilidza, and we reconnaissanced the area. We met with the leaders, and they were happy to meet Morillon there. But we did not hear of any war or any fighting. It was a peaceful atmosphere, and we were discussing the facilities that they could provide for Morillon and his command. After that, we visited the Kiseljak area, and he found it to be more suitable. But I recall that while we were in Ilidza to conduct this dialogue with the commanders there, we did hear that such events had taken place. They may have taken place somewhere else. But I believe it was completely calm when we were there. This is what I recall, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more matter. Do you agree that in the course of visits of high-ranking UNPROFOR officials, the other side would provoke? And this document shows that our side had losses for lightly-wounded soldiers, but in spite of these losses, our side did not return fire. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was the decision made, I highly appreciate that decision. But in order to answer that question, I say that during my presence along with General Morillon in the Ilidza area, during our talks I think the weather was great, the atmosphere was great, and everything went fine. Everybody was happy for our presence. It was peaceful. We didn't hear any fire -- shots. We didn't receive any reports about any events. Perhaps there were some incidents away -- far away, but we did not hear of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D502, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D01252, 1D01252. I believe we only have the English version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
