utterances.text: General, you have already referred to this incident. This is a note to the Secretary-General. It concerns a visit to UNPROFOR. Could we have a look at page 4, the bottom of page 4. This paragraph concerns a report from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Please have a look at item 12, which is about the results of the Italian investigation into the crash of the aid plane. Do you remember that this plane was shot down somewhere above Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, I think it was shot down over Croatian territory. That's what I remember. We -- the incident was reported to us during our meeting with you in the area of Lukavica, when one of my aids whispered to me during the meeting that there was a crash. One plane was shot down en route to Sarajevo. I reported the incident to Mr. Goulding, and that's why we urgently ended the meeting and went back to our headquarters to follow the incident.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have a look at the next page, and I would like to ask everyone to read through this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Goulding says that if this was a deliberate act in order to provoke anger in the Western media and make a military intervention more likely, a military intervention for which they still hanker. Well, my question is do you remember that the possibility of this having been done by the Serbs was excluded because it was too far into the Croatian and Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in my reports about the incident, all of -- I said that the incident was reported to us, and I sent the chief of staff, Colonel Bederkenko [phoen], the sector chief of staff, along with a number of officers, to inquire the situation and to bring back a report. I didn't say who was behind the attack. I think that needed an advanced technical investigation to identify the perpetrator, while the incident could happen unprovoked due to a technical error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you remember that on the basis of that incident, there was a -- we were banned from using air-space? There was a no-fly zone order that was issued; yes or no, General? It's not a big question, but do you remember that this incident was used as a basis for a no-fly ban?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was a no-fly ban and only humanitarian aid planes were allowed in the space. No military purposes were accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the middle of paragraph 13, it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, you didn't answer to the question whether that ban was triggered by this incident which is reflected in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, the no-fly zone was already imposed. Only humanitarian aid planes were allowed. There was no air-space activities in that area because the operations were only terrestrial in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To be more precise, General: Do you remember that this incident was used as a basis to exert pressure on us so that we would move our planes to Yugoslavia? That would be a more precise question. And this was an enormous task that we had to carry out?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was even yet more enormous for us, because there was a no-fly -- there was a ban on our flights for about a month. Due to that incident, all air operations -- humanitarian air operations were frozen, suspended, and we only received humanitarian aid by land. We were severely affected. I'm talking about us and also about civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the middle of paragraph 13, it says: [In English] " The Serb leader, Dr. Karadzic was more positive, but maintained his objection to the participation in UNPROFOR of any regional power, especially Turkey, or any country which occupied Yugoslavia during the Second World War, including Italy." You discussed this matter, but do you remember that we had a preference for Asian and African troops rather than troops from NATO countries. The leadership had no reservations with regard to the Egyptian Battalion, but they were afraid that someone in the field might believe that the Egyptians were biased?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did explain this in the past. I can speak extensively of the Egyptian Battalion. I was at the origin of setting up the Egyptian forces. I was appointed a commander in Egypt, and we have our own rules of engagement. We have our own rules to abide by. When I heard this talk in Bosnia, I said, Please do not propagate such false propaganda if you don't have any evidence to back it up. As for deploying particular forces from the UN there, I think this can be done in light of an agreement by the parties concerned, and those countries have the right to accept or oppose the participation and a particular process -- forces. However, there was no opposition to the presence of an Egyptian battalion or of any other battalion. I don't know why such things are being raised here. Those matters had no incidents, and I can confirm, not in my capacity as a Egyptian, but as a UN commander. I would say no Egyptian leader would violate the principles of the mission at hand and that no one would violate the principles upon which his mission is based. And I think our motto was to be impartial, and everyone has to accept that. You already said that you claim that because of the Muslim faith of the Egyptian Battalion, and I accepted that, but this doesn't mean that you have to oppose the presence of an Egyptian battalion or an Egyptian commander. I am Egyptian, and I -- and I told you that you knew I was an Egyptian, and you did not oppose my presence in the meeting. And you said it at the beginning of the meeting, and I appreciated what you said about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I wasn't sufficiently clear. You said that we suggested that there shouldn't be any Egyptians in the field because of their safety. I wanted to clarify what you have just confirmed. I wanted to say that the leadership didn't have any reservations with regard to Egypt, but we were afraid that someone in the field might have such reservations. But we didn't believe that you were biased. We have clarified that matter now. I'll show what I have in mind, in fact, when I show this next document, but let's have a look at item 14 now, which concerns the agreements that we reached in London with regard to heavy weapons. And Mr. Goulding says: [In English] "As regard the implementation of the Hogg Agreement, UNPROFOR succeeded on September 2nd in agreeing with Dr. Karadzic a definition of heavy weapons." [Interpretation] And then there's something down below: [In English] "He said that he had accepted the Hogg Agreement as a gesture to the conference, but the Muslims had since launched unceasing offensive, and he would only honour agreement if they stopped attacking his forces." [Interpretation] Do you agree that -- or do you remember, rather, that Mr. Goulding came to this conclusion in this letter?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, sir. What I do remember that at the beginning of the meeting, where Nambiar, he told me that the results of the conference -- of the London Conference were positive, and we talked about the presence of these heavy weapons in 11 positions, and that I was going to monitor these positions within the limit of my capacity. And you told me, and this is documented, you told me that you did not mean, and you said that in the meeting, you did not mean the collection -- that the United Nations should monitor the collection of the heavy weapons, but to monitor those heavy weapons. You said that the Muslims were in large numbers and that we should monitor the presence of heavy weapons. I reported this to General Nambiar, and we were told that what was agreed upon in London was not implemented the way we understood it. And that wasn't also understood by Mr. Goulding, and Mr. Goulding told what he understood to Mr. Nambiar. So there was an agreement to monitor the collection -- to monitor the heavy weapons. However, the things on the ground were different. You may remember, sir, that you preferred that since we were supposed to monitor the collection of heavy weapons, why shouldn't we also monitor light mortars, since those mortars can inflict losses on the buildings too. Moreover, when I received instructions from General Nambiar over what you declared in London, I started to study the possibility of providing enough monitors to carry the mission. We did not have enough monitors at the disposal of the United Nations, so we set up small units that we extracted from each battalion. We tried to -- we tried to train those monitors in order to make up for the penury of monitors that we had, and after this mission the small units were restored by their battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you see what Mr. Goulding says: [In English] "President Izetbegovic complicated matters by pretending that the Hogg Agreement covered all Serb-controlled heavy weapons in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I denied that this was the case and the co-chairman have since confirmed this with the British authorities. They have also determined that noon, 12 September, would be dead-line ...," and so on. General, in the original document from Minister Hogg, the term used is "supervision," not "control." Here it says "Serb-controlled heavy weaponry." It doesn't say "to control Serbian weapons." So this is what I was asking you about. Were the parties trying to gain advantage from the implementation of the agreement, and did this obstruct the implementation of that agreement? Do you agree with what Mr. Goulding says about complicating matters?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I understood from that, that the difference was over your interpretation, whether the term should be used is -- that should be used is "supervision" or "control." The matters were clear to me. "Supervision" meant to monitor the heavy weapons in position, and there was no question of collecting them, and that the heavy weapons should stay where they are, and that the role of the United Nations is to monitor those weapons and to carry out a role of verification. However, the collection is -- means to collect those heavy weapons in a certain area by the United Nations, and that the United Nations forces should see to it that these weapons are not used. What we asked for was that those batteries should be put in certain positions to facilitate our monitoring mission in particular areas, but none of those things were really implemented.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If you remember, the artillery was grouped or massed together at 11 places, but we allowed for supervision, not control, as had been agreed with Ambassador Hogg. Let's have a look at the last page so that we can see who actually drafted this. Thank you. Could this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D503, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see 1D2125, please. 1D2125. I'll read it out once it's up on the screen. The 17th of September, 1992. I'm not sure if we have a translation. The encircled part says: "The command of the UNPROFOR forces in Sarajevo, the Egyptian General Razek, yesterday stated at a press conference that he's shocked by the statement made by the rump Presidency of BiH, Ejub Ganic, in which the peace forces of the UN are described in an inappropriate way. General Razek emphasised that this was not a way to establish co-operation with UNPROFOR. Ganic appeared to be a reasonable man, but I am shocked now. I would like to remind him of the fact that this is not the way in which to co-operate. If we no longer have the understanding and support of the people, we will be everyone's enemy."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you were shocked and that this is what you, in fact, stated at a press conference in mid-September?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sir, I can confirm that. As I already said, we faced difficult circumstances there. In the aftermath of my meeting with Mr. Ganic, and after I reported to him about the killing of the French drivers, he adopted a rather offensive position against me. He made some declarations to the press, and those declarations did not help to appease the situation between the United Nations and the inhabitants. It was said that we were poor officers, coming from poor countries, and that the situation was getting worse and worse. And he even called us names. He said that we are blue beret officers, that we're more interested in gaining money rather than carrying out our mission. I was shocked by such statements. We had a stormy meeting, and I said, Come on, let's calculate it together. How can an officer -- an Egyptian officer, who lives very well in Egypt and who is well off in Egypt -- how could you accuse a man of my age, who cannot even take a shower here and who is suffering here along with all the soldiers, how can you accuse me on this? I even called for press conferences. I called the media to come and report on this, to report on the situation and living conditions of the United Nations forces. We gave statements, we made declarations, and everybody knew about our sacrifices, about our sufferings in the area. I think those statements shocked me, and I clarified that in one of the press conferences, and this led to improving relations between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us briefly when your secretary was wounded? Can you give us the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assistant was an Egyptian national, and he was my liaison assistant with the Egyptian Battalion because of the language barrier. This also enabled me to focus on disciplinary matters with the Egyptian Battalion. My assistant was an experienced officer, and he was injured in an attack on one of the headquarters of the companies of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that it was not properly interpreted into Arabic. Your secretary, a lady who was a Serb, when was she wounded? What month was that?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was injured during the shelling of the PTT building. I think her name was Ms. Gordana. She is a Serb, and she sustained injuries in a direct hit on the PTT building. She was in the restroom, and she sustained severe injuries to her nervous system. And the medical doctor, the French doctor at the PTT building, suggested her evacuation because she is not a UN staff member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us when, please. When did it happen, approximately?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date. There is a report containing the date, in possibly November, December, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellent, thank you. That will do. Could you please have a look at this now, what Ganic said on the 15th of September. "Oslobodjenje," on the 15th of September, carried a text by Ejub Ganic, and the title was "The Dark Side of UNPROFOR." It says that: "UNPROFOR is bringing secretaries from Belgrade, young girls of marrying age, whose lack of knowledge of the English language is compensated by wonderful looks and a beautiful walk. Ganic says that they are also well-versed in espionage. He wrote about members of UNPROFOR, that they were disoriented, politically uninformed, without a mandate to think with their own heads. Foreign reporters --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't hear. There's no translation. I just hear Mr. Karadzic. There is no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, separate from the matter, what are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading from a document, from the very same document, the document that's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the second bit when you look at this box. First, it was what the general said, and below is what Ganic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see, because he noted it's from "Oslobodjenje," and the title of this document says "Glas" or something, because of that I was confused. But now, General, do you follow -- do you hear the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do hear the interpretation now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your last question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to read this out to see what was it that General Razek was reacting to. This is what was stated about the secretaries, the Serb women who were coming from Belgrade to UNPROFOR. Should I repeat the entire paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's up to you. I will read out the question for you: "It was titled --" It is Mr. Karadzic's question: "The title was 'The Dark Side of UNPROFOR.' It says that: "UNPROFOR is bringing secretaries from Belgrade, young girls of marrying age, whose knowledge of the English language is compensated by wonderful looks and a beautiful walk. Ganic says that they are also well-versed in espionage. He wrote about members of UNPROFOR, that they were disoriented, undisciplined, without a mandate to think with their own heads." Now, what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that part of what had angered you?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have to say something here. This is part of the work of the UN. A commander or a leading official of the UN has the discretion to use the services of locals. This is part of the UN's association with the local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree with that. However, was it these words of Ganic's that had angered you, inter alia? We're not challenging anything. We are just asking whether this is what had angered you, what he said.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In fact, Ganic was livid because I said the source of fire was the Presidency. This made his angry, and he responded in the way he did. I, personally, did not feel happy about the way he described the situation. That's why I said to him, You do not know how -- what our living conditions are, and if you want to send your own people to have a look at the way we lived in our headquarters, then they can do that. We treated locals with utmost respect. She was a respectable lady, this Ms. Gordana. She worked long hours. I think they did not understand how we operated, they did not see how we operated. At the time, I did not really notice these statements, so I'm not aware of what he said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is how foreign correspondents characterised this: "Foreign correspondents believe that this is a new step in the media campaign against the peace forces of the UN in Sarajevo, after open statements made --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No interpretation, no interpretation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you slow down when you put your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, on top on this, it's not clear where Mr. Karadzic is reading from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last part of this very same document, in the box. It is the last paragraph in that box. [In English] "Strani" means "foreign." [Interpretation] "Foreign correspondents believe that this is a new step in the media campaign against the peace forces of the United Nations in Sarajevo, after open statements made by UNPROFOR that it was the Muslim forces that were responsible for a series of attacks in town, especially the attack against the humanitarian convoy of the UN in which two French soldiers were killed." You had already confirmed that, that they were furious or livid because you had established that they were shooting all over town and at the convoy. Thank you. Now, so can this be admitted now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D21 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If we follow our guide-line, I have no problem in admitting the first part. But the second part is related to a third party's statement, which I don't think the witness has confirmed the content of it, but I speak for myself. I consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If I could just be heard briefly, because we've been admitting entire documents when the witness has only recognised some parts of it, so I think that it would be consistent with your guide-lines to admit the entire document, even though not all of it was confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the subject matters are totally different ones, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's true, but that's also been the case in other documents, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say a word. I did not put this question. The general, himself, confirmed this in advance. He said that Ganic was livid on account of what this last paragraph says, that they had established that it was the Presidency forces that were firing. So that was confirmed in advance. I just reinforced what the general had said, himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was not sure whether the general's comment was related to that. But with that understanding, we'll admit it, but being marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D504, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D2126, please. It has to do with this last paragraph, actually. This is from "The Independent." It's the 18th of January, 1993, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we can see here that they are quoting you, that you suggested to the Security Council to give the opposing sides an ultimatum, ordering them to pull back their forces, et cetera. However, it says here General Abdel-Razek said -- [In English] "... no intervention would solve the problems engendered by civil war." [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down a bit. General, do you see that paragraph towards the bottom: "General Abdel-Razek ..."?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we zoom in a bit further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's precisely what we have on our screen now. [In English] It said: "No intervention would solve the problems engendered by a civil war. Intervention would be very complicated ... peace should come through the will of the people concerned, he said. But now the opposing forces were enjoying killing each other and destroying everything with the world just standing by."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So implicitly, one can see that you had wanted intervention -- or, rather, you were against intervention and you wanted the opposing sides to show a goodwill to stop killing each other; right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not in a press conference. Maybe that was part of an interview. As you know, several correspondents lived with us, and they wanted to glean information from speaking to commanders. So maybe that was what I said in an interview with one of the correspondents, and this is a personal view, and I believed that an intervention would involve a wider scale of the use of force, and there were not sufficient forces on the ground. Therefore, I felt that there was a need for greater pressure from the Security Council, and again this is a personal feeling, a personal view. This pressure by the Security Council would lead to a cessation of hostilities and then to use the good officers to try and resolve the situation. This was my personal view and did not have any bearing on my position as a UN commander.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the third column towards the bottom as well. So can we have this same page zoomed in, but the third column. I'll read it out. It has to do with those attacks, and it says -- and it says that two soldiers of the French Foreign Legion were injured: "In conversation, French officers emphasised ..." [In English] " ... that Muslim forces have been responsible for many attacks on UN forces in Sarajevo. They also claim that the Bosnian leadership keeps water supplies limited to strengthen the siege mentality and make the city the focus of international attention."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that that is what we were saying all along and that we were disbelieved until the representatives of the international community saw this for themselves?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. What's the question in this -- in this, this part of the -- of the war games being played?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the question -- yes. We were saying that the Muslims were playing tricks on us and that they wanted us to be accused of victimising the city; as the French people say here, to strengthen this siege mentality. However, we were not believed until the foreigners experienced this, themselves; right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I have been clear in my dealings with actions of this nature. I used to report about these incidents. When I was asked to pin-point responsibility for certain actions, I would sit with my advisers and try to establish the facts, and base my report on these facts. And when we used to point the finger at the parties and holding them responsible for starting the shooting, they, of course, would deny that. Denial was a trademark of all the parties that we had to deal with, and this eventually led to the frustration I felt, because we found ourselves in a situation where we could not take action. We found ourselves turning in a vicious circle.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D505, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2127, please, could we have that now. It has to do with the same topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a letter of yours. I hope that we have the original as well. Actually, we don't know whether we have the English version, but this is a letter of yours sent to Colonel Siber, deputy chief of staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 19th of January, 1993. The subject of the letter is "Threat to the City." UNPROFOR headquarters, through UN observers, received information that in Blazuj -- do you remember where Blazuj is, General?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names of places cause me a lot of confusion. I am not sure if that's one of the areas that had major incidents and we had to deal with, to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you remember, it's when you go from Ilidza towards Hadzici. However, the transcript did not reflect the word "reservoir," that in Blazuj, the fuel reservoir was shelled on the 13th of January, 1993. "On the next day, officers from the Logistics Department carried out an on-site investigation in order to assess whether the damage caused may constitute environmental threat. The latest shelling of these installations was carried out by 120-millimetre mortars from positions on Mount Igman." And then we see here what remains. However, the last paragraph says: "I wish to inform you about the conclusions or findings of the investigation team that are as follows. Direct hits of the installations of the Blazuj reservoir, with the capacity of 45.000 tons of fuel and 300 cubic metres of gas, may result in considerable water pollution in town, because the River of Rakovica flows towards Sarajevo and is only about 100 metres away from the fuel reservoir." You signed it. It says: "H.A. Razek, Brigadier General, Commander Sector Sarajevo." Do you remember this letter that you sent to Colonel Siber?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do and. And as I said earlier, if an incident took place on the site, then we would report that incident to HQ. I used to speak to Galic, to Mladic, and to your command. I also spoke to the other side, to the command of the other side, in the same manner. And you will see that these same conversations reached the upper echelons of Galic's command. What we did -- our role was to bring the serious incidents to the attention of the supreme commanders on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just briefly, do we agree the Muslim forces were on Mount Igman, or, rather, the forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as people say, and that that was the reason why you wrote to Colonel Siber; right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D506, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. It's time for a break. General, I forgot to mention, when you began your testimony, but probably you must have been advised by the Victim and Witness Section, so during the breaks, until your testimony is over, you are not supposed to discuss about your evidence with anybody else. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll have a break for an hour. We'll resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Last week, when I announced that the Chamber would sit from 9.00 to 2.30 instead of 9.00 to 3.00, I thought it would apply to the future sitting in general, but I wasn't clear enough. But that was the Chamber's intention, that given that two members of the Bench are still being involved in other cases, so that they could have another time to meet in the afternoon, only when the courtroom is available. So given the circumstances, we need to rise for today at quarter to 3.00. And then I understand that there's a matter to raise on your part, Mr. Robinson, so I would like Mr. Karadzic to conclude his cross for today at 3.35 -- 2.35. I'll let you know. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If possible, could we now see the video. 1D2144 is the number. My assistant shall show it for us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "There's no use anybody pretending that there are innocents in this business and that there is one side that is pure white, the victims, and the other side pure wrong, black, the aggressors. That is not the case."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you able to follow what Lord Owen was saying, General? Are you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you able to follow what Lord Owen was saying?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with his position?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally had a discussion over lunch with Lord Owen on some issues, and his opinion was that everybody is liable, everybody is to blame, and this was his opinion. He said this to me in a private discussion. He said, Everybody is responsible, and we have to stop this irresponsible situation. He was -- he is a diplomat, a diplomatic person, who does not make pronunciations that could be understood to be an accusation directed at this or that party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we continue viewing this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Lord Carrington, as mediator for the European Community, and with a reputation as a hard-line critic of the Bosnian Serbs. But Owen quickly learned that Muslim forces routinely staged incidents to turn world opinion against the Serbs. Media reports, for instance, had accused the Serbs of targeting Kosevo Hospital in Sarajevo." "The UN Monitors actually saw a mortar bomb -- a mortar crew come into the hospital, and Bosnian gunmen, military forces in uniform, and fire over the Kosevo Hospital into an area presumably Serb. The vehicle was packed up very quickly. A television crew arrived, set up in the grounds of the hospital, and a few minutes later retaliatory fire came on the place where the mortar came and, of course, landed on or near the hospital, all filmed on television."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this, in fact, your point of view as well, and General Morillon wrote about this to Izetbegovic and protested about violations of the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he also addressed -- he also wrote to the Serbian side about certain events. As soon as we gathered information about certain incidents, we wrote about them, and we addressed directly the command related to the matter, whether on the Bosnian side or on the other side. And I know, from my discussions with General Morillon, that he did write such a letter addressed to the Bosnian leadership on the misuse of their forces -- the mis-deployment of their forces next to civilian facilities. And I discussed this matter with Mr. Ganic, and he would say, Where can we go? The whole area is full of buildings and civilians. Where can we go to defend ourselves? And this was his point of view. I always underlined, Please do not deploy military forces next to UN facilities, and no military forces be deployed next to important facilities, so that we may avoid this ongoing outcry about the attacks against civilian facilities and civilians, who were heavily impacted by -- as a result.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we continue viewing this video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Owen learned a strong-worded letter had been sent to the government of Alija Izetbegovic by the UN Commander in Sarajevo, General Philippe Morillon, stating: 'I now have concrete evidence from witnesses of this disreputable and cowardly act. I must point out to you the harm that such blatant disregard for the Geneva Convention does to your cause.'" "When I said to General Morillon, who was, I think, an exceptionally able soldier in every way, Well, why didn't you make this public, he shrugged his shoulders in a little [indiscernible] way and said, We were comitted."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with what Lord Owen said? He said that life in Sarajevo was such and the situation was such that General Morillon and other international representatives couldn't publicly exert pressure on the Presidency in order to put an end to these violations of the Geneva Conventions, and the fact that people lived there was important when it came to making such announcements?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say we are a military personnel. We do not apply pressures. We only file reports about events that took place. And we asked them to investigate the issue and not to repeat such actions. We informed the leadership, and then the leadership has the ability to co-ordinate with the personal envoy of the Secretary-General and with the envoy of the European Community, too, and they, in turn, would apply political pressures against the relevant leaderships. Our role was only inform the leadership of what we witnessed. And here we are speaking of specific events, and, as I believe, many of the matters took place in this way. Each person had his own opinion. But I personally believed, and as I said before, that this is a war game, and everybody denied the fact that he carried out any of these actions. Every single time we informed a party that such an event took place and that our reports from our observers show that the shelling had its source here or there, everybody answered in the same way. This was a war game, in general, in the Sarajevo region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree with what you have said, but the problem is that UNPROFOR and the international representatives could always publicly comment on the Serbian side -- object to the Serbian side, but with regard to the Muslim side, such objections couldn't be made public, and that is what we saw in what Lord Owen said. And as a result, a certain picture was painted according to which the Serbs were the bad guys, whereas the other side only had good guys, they were the victims. So the media was biased against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the bias was not from the media. The media was able to move very freely in the region. They followed events and developments. You know the area was full of correspondents of the media, representatives of radio, television, and printed press, as in any other conflict zone in the world. I know that such an intense presence of the media is normal, and it is part of the job. I was not concerned with one side or the Serbs being stigmatised as the bad side, et cetera. As the Chamber has just heard, I said this before, whenever I saw an error committed by any one of the parties, I reported this, whether by the Bosnian side or by the Serb side. I wrote about it and I discussed it with them, and I said, Such and such an event took place. Now, what the politicians said, the politicians who toured the area, that's up to them. I was a field commander, and I only wrote about what I witnessed, and I reported about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I only wanted to say that it would have helped, perhaps, if General Morillon had published this letter. I believe you would have published, because you were very severe with Ganic. Let's continue viewing this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would only like to add here that at a certain stage of our work, I would address letters to General Morillon as responsible for the Sarajevo Sector, but he had responsibilities for the overall region of Bosnia. I only reported on what concerned the Sarajevo Sector.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we continue viewing this excerpt, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "... in his little [indiscernible] way, and he said, We were comitted." "Lord Owen and UN mediator Cyrus Vance found that their efforts to negotiate a compromise to end the conflict were undermined by the propaganda war that targeted US public opinion." "... remark, They have a press and a television presentation that it's still cowboys and Indians, good and bad. They like to see things in simple terms, so there's no doubt about that, as being helped by some very strongly-motivated propaganda. It's a propaganda war as well as an actual physical war."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that a propaganda war was being played out as well, and the Serbs were stated to be the losers in that war? It was said that they weren't capable of waging a war in the sphere of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not find that I have a response to this question. I am not specialised in the media. In fact, on a personal level, I have my diploma in media, but when the media is somewhere, based somewhere and covers events, and as I said in the session yesterday, perhaps the error was on your side, because you own the heavy weapons, but you do not own the capability to clarify your positions. And I said, on my part, I asked the correspondent of CNN in the sector at that time to have an -- to interview you, and I believe she did so. And if you have a case, then tell her. And I did this also with Ganic, and I am speaking of Christiane Amanpour from the CNN. This is how things happened. The media was all around us, and I tried, as far as possible, to let each side tell his story, and the world will understand and will know, and perhaps this could help the situation in the field that concerned me most. But you cannot impose on the media what to say or what to do. They have their own cameras, they have their own methods, and they take news from here or from there, in their own ways, and they have many ways to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thanks to you, Ms. Amanpour was granted an interview by me on several occasions. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that I said, The man appears to be a bad guy, but go and ask him all your questions. Tell him, This and this is said about you, and listen to his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me -- in the course of the interview, we agreed that the international public stated or claimed that the Serbs were the aggressors, but you opposed that view because you were convinced that it was a civil war in which it was difficult to control everything in the field? Could you answer by just say "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said this more than once. I said this is a civil war taking place between neighbours and neighbourhoods, and we are right in the middle of these battles. I do not distinguish one side from the other here. I describe it as it is. It was a civil war. And as I told you, I was not concerned with what took place along the front-lines. I was concerned with what happened to the civilians inside Sarajevo, within the context of the agreement signed between the different relevant parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We also agreed that you were aware of the fact that I always wanted to help you fulfill your mandate. That was my sincere desire, and I strove to ensure that that was possible.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said this once and again. The discussion with you was positive, and you always agreed to what we presented and what we asked of you and of your forces. The main dilemma was in how we saw this translated in the field. This was what concerned us most. We did not see much on the field. We would say, Why do we find so many claims, then? And this was the war game, as I call it, where I hear nice words and warm welcomes and words of readiness, but when I go to the field, I find something very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's for that reason that my associate asked you whether you had the impression that I was trying to deceive you, and you said that the difference between desires and the situation in the field wasn't a result of deception, but it was the result of the nature of that civil war?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that anyone was deceiving me. As a professional general, I know very well that such matters take place because this is a civil war, and I know very well that there will be many problems. And all I asked the parties I talked to was to discipline their soldiers, to control their soldiers in the field, so that what we agree on will be implemented, because this situation is going on and on. Every time, we have a nice dialogue and nice decisions and a positive response and agreement, but then we discover that events take another line. But I never said that anyone was deceiving me. There is a personal chemistry among people, and from my discussions with you and from the numerous meetings, I felt that you were keen on having these matters take place in order to improve your image before public opinion. I realise this. However, the problem was in the chain of command. How do all these good intentions reach down to the soldiers? I believe this was a big problem, and this was a [indiscernible] of the crisis in the Sarajevo region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of the Chamber and the other participants, let's remind ourselves of the fact that you confirmed that in the event of an attack against army positions, a soldier didn't need a particular order to return fire to defend himself.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find these things are normal, they happen. But then they are the leaders. If anything happens, then their commanders should contain matters. Otherwise, it means there is a problem in the chain of command, and this means that low-level soldiers will create a crisis on the leadership level. If anything goes wrong, leaders should contain matters, control matters, and let things go back to normal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D214, please. Your Excellency, will this video be admitted into evidence? We have particular excerpts, discreet excerpts, so it's not necessary to determine the time-frame. We can provide the Registry with the relevant information now or with the relevant excerpts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you identify what programme it was?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is from the film made by an American director whose name is Bogdanic. But we're not suggesting that the comments be admitted into evidence; only what was stated by Lord Owen. The film is called "The War That Could Have Been Avoided." I think it's available, and I think that we will be using certain other excerpts from that film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know where it was broadcast?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that it was broadcast on this private television in Bosnia called PN, but it was broadcast several times on different TV stations. It is an authorised film and is sold as such. We have the film in its entirety, and we can make it available to all. I believe that we're going to be using other clips during these proceedings as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, no objections against the use of the speech of David Owen, but not the entire video. Just the David Owen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. On that part, that excerpt will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D507, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have 1D214, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, General, may I inform you of the following: This is our appeal to all Serb officers from Bosnia who haven't come yet, and now I'm just going to read one paragraph from that document. It pertains to what you spoke of a few moments ago in relation to the possibility of control and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, now we have it. But only in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, yes, only in B/C/S. I shall read it, and the interpreters can confirm that. The Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Presidency, the 6th of August, 1992. The heading is "An Appeal to All Serb Military Officers to Place Themselves at the Disposal of the Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Could we please have the next page. The middle of the next page, yes. I'll just read out part of it: "How do you feel when you know that instead of you, companies and brigades are led by teachers, workers, economists, professors, and you are seeking safety where there is no war? You have ceded your own place to people with a big heart, and kept your knowledge all for yourselves."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This desperate plea -- appeal of the Presidency to officers from Bosnia-Herzegovina to come back and to command, does it not confirm to you that we did not have enough professional officers and that units were led by amateurs, people of different occupations?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, when I contacted the Serbian leaders, I met with highly-professional officers, and that was obvious to me. They were in uniform, their military appearance was professional, they were disciplined, and their behaviour. And on the ground, I also met with professional soldiers who were deployed in different areas, carrying their weapons, in their own vehicles. I also met with civilians, armed civilians. I was intercepted by a number of groups from that particular category from both sides. It was obvious that it was a civil war, where civilians mixed with the military. That was the nature of the war. I really understood the situation, but that was -- that was not a desert -- the front-line was not a desert; it was a city. So the situation, as it was, was, for me, understandable. You complained once to me that you had few troops on the ground and that you needed to keep your weapons. That's what you said to me. And the other side said that the civilians were defending their own homes. And you said that, and the other side was saying what they said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted; for identification, that is? I believe that it needs to be translated in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D508, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D3128, please. 1D3128, please. Yes, that's it. Can we just have it in the center, because I believe that we don't have a translation into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is towards the very end of your tour of duty, the 31st of January, 1993; right? Can it please be zoomed in so that the general can see.

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this document was issued by the end of my tour of duty. I left Sarajevo by February.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have page 3 of this document. Sorry, could we first have page 2. A bit further down, where it says "Others." I'm going to read it out in English now: [In English] "One UNPROFOR, 20 UNHCR flights landed at the airport. "UNHCR convoy (7 unloaded trucks) escorted today to Pale. "Electricity repair mission in Golo Brdo was cancelled due to lack of cease-fire in the area. "Colonel General Morozov, Ukrainian defence minister, inspected the UkrBat and left Sarajevo at 11.25. "Food deliveries still go in Sarajevo, Butmir, Grbavica. "One UNMO post (Papa 5) was successfully evacuated due to heavy shelling." [Interpretation] Can we have page 3. [In English] "Convoy escorting will continue. "B. One water repair mission in Bacevo was planned. "Food delivery will be continued." And so on and so on. [Interpretation] Could we now have page 4, please. If you remember, General, you did have a look at this report about outgoing and incoming fire, and number 1 says that: "The following outgoing fire was observed from Serb positions: "Artillery: 41. "Mortars: 47. "Tank: 25. "And rockets: 25. As for Muslim territory, that is to say, territory under the control of -- oh, sorry, yes, from the Muslim positions, this is Lima, this is Papa, right: [In English] "Artillery, 196 [realtime transcript read in error "126"]." Mortar is 26; tanks, nil; rockets, 105; and AAA, 19. And let us see now incoming fire that was observed on the Serb-controlled territory: "Artillery: 26. "Mortars: 124." Tanks, nothing, rockets and AAA, nothing. And let's see the following incoming fire that was observed on the Presidency-controlled area: "Artillery: 104. "Mortar: 344. "Tanks: 3." Rocket and AAA, nil and nil. [Interpretation] As for point 2, it is 196. I seem to have read out "126," but we can all see this document. It says "196."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can we explain, and if so, how, that the Muslim side fired 196 artillery shells, and out of those 196 shells, only 26 fell on Serb territory? Where are the remaining 170 shells?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that might be a slight disingenuous -- excuse me, General. A slight disingenuous question. It says the following: "Incoming fire was observed on Serb-controlled areas." It doesn't rule out the possibility that shells landed on Serb-controlled areas, but was not observed. So it's a very difficult question for anyone to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But then, Excellency, these reports cannot be taken into account as evidence in a criminal case; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it's you who's seeking to put them into evidence. I simply observe what the document says and the inevitable inferences one has to draw from the plain language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to hear the general's comment, and I would like to tender this report not in terms of what happened, but I'm just trying to say that these reports practically don't mean a thing unless an investigation is carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, isn't there a considerable difference here? The Serbs fired 41, and the Presidency -- on the Presidency side, 104 shells fell. And 26 shells fell on Serb territory out of 196 that were fired. It's an enormous discrepancy, isn't it? Don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to clarify this piece of information. We have what is called sitrep, which is the daily report of the sector activities. We have monitors who are deployed in various positions, but they cannot cover all positions. So I would say in these reports "approximately," I would use the term "approximately." During my tour of duty, I asked for electronic means that would help us determine the source of the fire. I think there was one apparatus which was out of order by the Ukrainian -- owned by the Ukrainian Battalion. I think that some side would report some of these shells and miss some other shells, so I think those reports would say that the percentage of the fire from this side was probably more important than that coming from the other side. So I always insisted in my conclusions that the report was only approximate. I hope that I have been able to clarify this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's quite clear to me, and I hope that it's clear to the Trial Chamber and all the other participants. Let me ask you, though: Do you allow for the possibility that intentionally or by error, part of these artillery shells from the Muslim side fell on the Muslim side, itself?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all what I have mentioned, I think it would be difficult to investigate the question. I wish you could take into consideration our capabilities, which were not commensurate with what we were expected to do. So when we reported any shelling against a United Nations-controlled position, those reports were corroborated by the Serbians. So those were our reports, and I think we could not do much more. That was the situation in the Sarajevo Sector. I would like to reiterate that if we go back to these reports, we can tell from those reports that many shells originated from the Serbian-controlled areas, so we wanted to verify where those shells fell. And our monitors verified that shells and mortar shells, heavy shells, landed in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Had you the same attitude towards Muslim shells as well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am not taking sides with any side. I was working with my subordinates in the command. We all agreed on the kind of report to be sent, in light of profound analysis of the information that we had at our disposal, information which was provided by professional officers. And then we sent our reports to our headquarters. We did understand that we are in the middle of the war and that there was no understanding on a cease-fire. However, there were agreements by both sides to facilitate the mission of the United Nations forces in time of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, we certainly cannot rule out the possibility of some artillery shells having been fired from one side, simply fell on their own territory. We cannot rule that out; right?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, I am not saying this with absolute certainty. I think we draw our reports in accordance with the information at our hand, and we conclude our reports by saying that the report -- or the information included in the report was approximate. And if you refer to my reports, you could verify that for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, rest assured that I'm not criticising either the United Nations or Egypt, least of all you, personally. The transcript does not reflect what you said, Nothing was accurate. You did say that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I meant, but I didn't say, with absolute certainty, that the information about the shells was absolutely accurate. But there are technical means which would have given us accurate information, but we did not have those electronic means. So that's why I say that the information is approximate and are tantamount to be accurate. So I don't think the information was imaginative, but as near to the truth as possible. So we did not have the military capability to precisely identify the source of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Rest assured that I'm not criticising either the United Nations or Egypt, least of all you, personally. I am just trying to establish this relativity that you established just now. However, during the interview, you also said to me that shelling, as far as the bread line and the tram, et cetera, was concerned, did not involve investigations and that, for criminal law purposes, it would have been better had investigations been carried -- investigations been carried out, rather than having these reports that can be partially accurate?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did investigate the incidents, themselves, but we did not have the capacity to investigate all targets to verify the source of fire. That was not our mission. We reported the incidents generally, like, for example, the market-place was shelled, and then we would draw a link between the incident and the source of fire. So we would not be absolutely accurate as to identify the source of fire. There was also some shortage in finding a link between the incident and the shelling. So I don't at all doubt what you are saying, given our previous relationship. I know that you have -- you did have good relations with me and you have a good attitude towards the United Nations. I didn't say anything contrary to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D509, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D1222. At the same time, it is P1006. Let us just briefly deal with this. Let us try to refresh our memories. Yes, yes. I hope that there is a translation, too, because this is a Prosecution exhibit. Thank you. It's the Command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to the command of other units, various units. You see this line in the Serbian text and what is inserted there. It means that it is sent to all units, and then the name of a particular unit is entered there. Can we have paragraph 18 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 18, I'm going to read it out in Serbian, and we can see it in English too. General Galic and Colonel Krsmanovic are sending this order to their subordinate units, and paragraph 18 pertains to UNPROFOR, and it says: "The attitude towards members of UNPROFOR, foreign journalists, must be as correct and as civilised as possible, and make it possible for them to see our good sides and present it to our advantage." Since this has already been admitted, do you remember these efforts made by professional officers that you be received with due respect? You have confirmed, yourself, that at Ilidza, the Serbs welcomed you properly and with due respect?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have said this repeatedly. I had no problem whatsoever with the leadership, and even with General Galic, himself. I did attract his attention to a few matters; that he should be strict in issuing his orders to his subordinates; that his orders should be seen through. And I told him that, By seeing your orders through by your own troops would improve the image of the Serbs, in terms of respecting us and behaving -- and showing us good behaviour. I think you should find the political solution to the problem elsewhere. I always reiterated that I was dealt with in a proper, civilised manner, and I continue to reiterate that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D2122. This confirms what you have just been saying about a civilised and courteous relationship. This is a greeting you sent to General Galic, who was promoted to the rank of a general. So you, in fact, congratulated him on that fact. We can also have a look at the English version. Here, it say for Major General Stanislav Galic, from General Hussein Ali Abdel-Razek on the 2nd of January, 1993: "It's an honour for me to congratulate you on your promotion to the rank of major general. "I wish to present you with my compliments of the personnel and members of the UNPROFOR - Sarajevo Sector - and their wishes for a long, healthy, and happy life with the hope for peace. "General Hussein Ali Abdel-Razek."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember sending this letter of congratulations?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we are professional soldiers, and this is common practice that professional soldiers exchange congratulations on their promotion. And you, personally, remember I came to wish you a Merry Christmas. These are courteous approaches, and we are used to these practices in our professional life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to joke a little, when generals are in favour of peace, that results in them losing their jobs; isn't that correct? When generals are in favour of peace, when two generals want peace, then they are working against themselves. This would be to the detriment of their profession. Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D510, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D2146. Do we have that much time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be your last question for today, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D2146.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is from Srna, news from Srna. It says: "The Serbian side accepted the suggestion that a certain belt should be demilitarised, a belt of a thousand metres around the Sarajevo Airport, and that would solve the problem of using the Sarajevo Airport in a permanent way for humanitarian aid to be delivered. This is one of the most important details from the meeting held yesterday in Lukavica between the Egyptian general, Hussein Abdel-Razek, the commander of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, and between Colonel Galic. The problem of the abuse of UNPROFOR units by Muslim formations was also discussed. They opened fire on Serbian positions and use as a shield buildings and equipment that belonged to units from UNPROFOR. Opening a corridor so that citizens from Sarajevo could get out of Sarajevo and towards Belgrade and Split was also discussed. UNPROFOR was informed of the massacre that was carried out by Muslim extremists against Serbs in the Sarajevo settlement of Dogredi [phoen]. They were also informed of the fact that the Muslim side is mobilising Serbs into its army and sending it into the first combat lines, and they arrest those who refuse to do this."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this meeting at which you obtained this significant objective? A 1.000-metre belt around the airport was cleared of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember I raised this issue in one of the meetings with General Galic, in addition to other topics. And when I used to meet with General Galic, I used to go through another officer, and I believe his name was Lakic, about what to be discussed at meetings. This specific point did not see any positive developments between the two sides and remained one of the contentious issues. And as I said earlier, one of the main mission statements of the UNPROFOR was to protect the airport and its personnel, and that's why we met with the other parties -- with the two parties in the -- at the airport, because we wanted to create that demilitarised area. And it was an idea by General Morillon, and we wanted to ensure that the UN enjoyed that protection, but to the date of my departure, there was no improvement. I recall that there were certain pieces that were withdrawn from under the foliage cover that they were under, but other pieces remained there, and the area was always susceptible to skirmishes and armed engagements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, would you agree that the Butmir settlement, where SDA soldiers were located, is 50 metres from the airport, and they never accepted this; whereas, Colonel Galic [as interpreted] accepted this suggestion, but the other side refused to accept it? And since both sides did not accept this, it wasn't possible to implement it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I took this issue to Mr. Galic [as interpreted], and I told him that the commander in the Butmir area is not up to the task and that he has been creating all kinds of problems for us. And he took that on board, and I believe that the commander of the Butmir area was replaced. And we have always stated this. We believe that Butmir area was a source of a lot of problems for us. And we asked for the replacement of the commander, and that is -- that was exactly what happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted into evidence? And for the sake of the transcript, it's not "Mr. Galic" - Mr. Galic is an officer - but "Mr. Ganic," the vice-president of the Muslims. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be marked for identification as Exhibit D511. General, we'll stop here. We'll adjourn here for today, and then we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. So you may go now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. This is a motion for reconsideration of your decision concerning the commencement of the cross-examination of the witness Ekrem Suljevic, as well as the duration of that cross-examination. And the new facts that we have to present to you is the fact that on Friday evening and on Monday, we received a lot of Rule 66(B) disclosure documents, including 41 that we've been able to identify as not having been received before, all authored by that witness, concerning different incidents of shelling and sniping. In addition, yesterday and today we received notice that the Prosecution will be using 45 additional documents as exhibits with the witness, relating to air bombs. And we feel that these developments warrant additional time for us both to prepare for the cross-examination as well as to conduct it, and so on that basis we would ask that the Chamber allow the direct examination of this witness to proceed, but postpone the cross-examination until after the recess, so that we've had an adequate opportunity to review the new disclosure as well as to conduct investigation, if necessary, on some of those incidents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, that would be an unfortunate and unnecessary and unfounded waste of the Court's time. Let me address the matters raised by Mr. Robinson. First of all, the assertion that there were 45 additional documents notified to the Defence is inaccurate. Those 45 documents appeared in the notification of June 8th, approximately six weeks ago, concerning the documents that would be used. What happened is that a statement was prepared dealing with those documents in conformity with the Court's guidance about the use of such documents and its professed interest in having witnesses, where possible, address them directly. Those documents, I might add, were previously the subject of either a Bar table submission or 94(B) submission. But, more importantly, as mentioned, they were incorporated in and notified by the notice to the Defence more than a month ago; indeed, approximately six weeks ago. Now, the upshot of taking the statement is a benefit to both the Court and the Defence. Now, instead of having these matters discussed as indicated in court and having to react to them on the spot, the Defence now knows what the witness says about those documents and can prepare in advance for that. So this is an aid to cross-examination, not a hindrance. It also provides the Court with the understanding of what the witness will say and an opportunity to ask any clarifying questions it might have about those matters. Now, with respect to the 60 -- the additional documents that Mr. Robinson mentioned with respect to 66(B), that was a very recent 66(B) request by the Defence, and while Mr. Robinson is free to make 66(B) requests that trigger broad disclosure at any time he wishes, it's hardly good cause for continuing cross-examination when the requested -- the request, indeed, turns up documents. These particular documents are not -- don't reflect incidents that the Prosecution intends to lead evidence on. As the Court is aware, Mr. Suljevic is an investigator. He participated in the investigation of any number of incidents, many of which the Prosecution is not leading evidence on. And I'm not entirely clear what the Defence -- why the Defence is seeking those or what it intends to do with it, but that's within its discretion. In any event, they are not incorporated by the evidence the Prosecution intends to lead. That evidence, as mentioned, was disclosed to the Defence long ago and notified approximately six weeks ago in early June. Thank you, Your Honour. So for those reasons -- let me mention one more, and that is that: Thus far during the course of the cross-examinations the accused has conducted, I think we've seen that he's ventured into areas that don't make for the most efficient cross-examination, and I think we can -- there's reason, based on the previous cross-examinations, to be confident that the time allotted here will be more than sufficient to deal with all the matters raised. As Judge Morrison has mentioned on a couple of occasions in connection with similar requests for extended time, the Court is in a position to deal with those matters when the time arrives based on the way in which the time was utilised, and the Court is in a similar position here. I -- we oppose continuing this matter or not proceeding with the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I do have to apologise. I now see that these documents were notified to us on the 8th of June, although we received the explanation for the witness's connection to these documents on Monday. So I stand corrected on that point. And I simply would inform the Chamber that the Rule 66(B) request was made on the 21st of June, which was about a month ago, so we just received these documents on Friday and Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A very quick point, Your Honour. We have talked to Mr. Robinson before about the resources involved in fulfilling these requests. He's well-aware of the fact that the turnaround is significant, especially when there are other 66(B) requests in line before it. I only mention that it's not a simple turnaround matter and is a matter of limited resources.

utterances.text: The Chamber needs to rise now, and we'll give our ruling tomorrow morning. Very briefly, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. I understand the fact that the Prosecution lacks certain resources, but please take into consideration the fact that the Defence's resources are far less than those of the Prosecution.
